content.text: : myocellular damage leads to myocardial necrosis & dysfunction, leading to HF
– fever, myalgias, malaise for several days followed by
– infiltration of lymphocytes w/ myocardial tissue necrosis
Inflammation of the pericardium, the outer layer of the heart
(worse when supine & improved w/ sitting forward)
•pain may radiate to back, shoulder, neck, arm, or epigastric area
: best heard at end expiration while upright & leaning forward
ST elevations in the precordial leads w/ associated PR depressions in those leads
because they can interfere w/ myocardial scar formation
Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space
Normally, about 5-15ml of fluid is in the pericardial space
: viral, idiopathic, immune, malignancy – lung cancer MC, breast second MC, aortic dissection, uremia
: test of choice – increased fluid in pericardial space
Pericardial effusion causing significant pressure on the heart, impeding cardiac filling, leading to decreased CO & shock
: complication of acute pericarditis or trauma; malignancy MC non-traumatic cause
: exaggerated (>10mmHg) ↓ in systolic pressure w/ inspiration
Dyspnea, fatigue, peripheral edema, shock, reflex tachycardia, cool extremities
: low voltage QRS complexes, electrical alternans
- volume resuscitation & pressor support if needed
Loss of pericardial elasticity (thickening, fibrosis, calcification) leading to
: fibrosis limits ventricular filling, decreased stroke volume & cardiac output
(the lack of an inspiratory decline or an ↑ in jugular vein pressure w/ inspiration)
: high pitched diastolic sound similar to S3 (sudden cessation of ventricular filling)
: pericardial calcification may be seen esp. on lateral view, clear lung fields
– early diastolic dip followed by a plateau if diastasis
for symptom relief as well as reduction of edema & venous pressure
